components.note: 咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'
忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他们之间的感情很深。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zhījiān de gǎnqíng hěn shēn.
example.english: The bond between them is deep.
example.fact: 感情 and 感觉 are frequently confused by learners since English “feelings” covers both: 感情 names an emotional bond or sentiment, often between people (谈感情, “to nurture a relationship”), while 感觉 covers a momentary sensory impression or hunch (一种奇怪的感觉, “a strange feeling”).

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
亻 (person) — relates to 候's meaning 'to wait, time,' as if a person watching and waiting.
矦 (hóu) gives a sound hint — 候 is pronounced hòu, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 我有时候会忘记吃早饭。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒushíhou huì wàngjì chī zǎofàn.
example.english: Sometimes I forget to eat breakfast.
example.fact: 有时候 is literally “there are times [when]” — 有 (“to have, there is”) plus 时候 (“time, moment”) — and is very often doubled as 有时候...有时候... to contrast two alternating situations, matching English “sometimes...sometimes...”

components.note: 龙 (dragon) — historically linked to layered ceremonial robes, extended to mean 'to inherit, pass down' and later 'to raid.'
衣 (yī) gives a rhyme close to xí, with a different initial.
手 (hand) — in the traditional form 擊, 手 contributed the meaning of striking with force, the source of 击's meaning 'to hit, strike.'

example.hanzi: 敌军在夜里发动了突然袭击。
example.pinyin: Díjūn zài yèli fādòng le tūrán xíjī.
example.english: The enemy troops launched a sudden attack at night.
example.fact: 袭's traditional form is linked to layered ceremonial robes and, by extension, to “inheriting, carrying on” a pattern — a sense that still surfaces in 沿袭 (“to carry on a tradition”) and 抄袭 (“to plagiarize,” literally “to copy and carry on”) — while 袭击 itself narrowed long ago to the “sudden raid, ambush” sense seen here.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 演 originally described water flowing and spreading out, later extended to 'developing, unfolding'
寅 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to 演's reading yǎn, having drifted apart over time
屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 今晚的演出非常精彩。
example.pinyin: Jīnwǎn de yǎnchū fēicháng jīngcǎi.
example.english: Tonight's performance was excellent.
example.fact: 演 alone already means “to perform, to act” (as in 表演), and 出 contributes a sense of “coming out, appearing” — together 演出 paints the fairly literal image of a performance “coming out” before an audience.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 她把一生都献给了教育事业。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ yìshēng dōu xiàngěi le jiàoyù shìyè.
example.english: She dedicated her whole life to education.
example.fact: 一生 is the more literary, written counterpart to the everyday spoken synonym 一辈子 (yíbèizi) — both mean “a whole lifetime,” but 一生 shows up far more in writing and formal speech, while 一辈子 dominates casual conversation.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.hanzi: 我一点儿都不在乎结果。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yìdiǎnr dōu bú zàihu jiéguǒ.
example.english: I don't care about the result at all.
example.fact: 不在乎 attaches directly to a noun or clause with no preposition needed (不在乎钱, “doesn't care about money”; 不在乎别人怎么说, “doesn't care what others say”) — a contrast with English “to care about,” which always needs “about” before its object.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呼 describes an action of the mouth, such as calling out or breathing.
乎 (hū) gives the sound — an exact match with 呼.
口 (mouth) — 吸 describes breathing in through the mouth.
及 (jí) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xī has diverged.

example.hanzi: 深呼吸可以帮助你放松。
example.pinyin: Shēn hūxī kěyǐ bāngzhù nǐ fàngsōng.
example.english: Deep breathing can help you relax.
example.fact: 呼 and 吸 individually mean “to exhale” and “to inhale” — 呼吸 fuses two opposite-direction breathing actions into one word for “to breathe,” a compounding pattern (pairing complementary opposites) also seen in words like 买卖 (“buy-sell,” meaning “business, trade”).

components.note: 日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.
日 (sun) — 星 relates to bright heavenly bodies like the sun and stars
生 (shēng) gives a sound close to 星's reading xīng

example.hanzi: 她是一位很受欢迎的电影明星。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi hěn shòu huānyíng de diànyǐng míngxīng.
example.english: She is a very popular movie star.
example.fact: 明星 literally means “bright star” (明 “bright” + 星 “star”) — the image of a celebrity as a bright, shining star in the sky lines up almost exactly with the same metaphor in English “star.”

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 超 relates to overtaking or surpassing someone while moving
召 (zhào) gives a sound distantly related to 超's reading chāo, having drifted apart over time
纟 (thread) — 级 originally named a strand or rank of silk thread, extended to 'grade, level, rank.'
及 (jí) gives the sound — 级 is also pronounced jí, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这部电影超级好看!
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng chāojí hǎokàn!
example.english: This movie is super good!
example.fact: 超 (“to exceed, surpass”) plus 级 (“grade, level”) literally means “exceeding the normal grade” — a transparent compositional root that made 超级 a natural fit both for coining terms like 超级市场 (“supermarket”) and, in casual speech, for use as a standalone intensifying prefix before an adjective (超级好, “super good”), echoing English “super-.”

components.note: 火 (fire) — linked to ritual fires once used to try to communicate with spirits
彐 (jì) gives a sound distantly related to 灵's reading líng, having drifted apart considerably over time
鬼 (ghost/spirit) — 魂 names a person's spirit or soul.
云 (yún) gives a rhyme close to hún, with a different initial.

example.hanzi: 音乐是这部电影的灵魂。
example.pinyin: Yīnyuè shì zhè bù diànyǐng de línghún.
example.english: Music is the soul of this film.
example.fact: 灵 and 魂 are near-synonyms that both independently can mean “spirit, soul” (灵 tied to ritual and the numinous, 魂 tied to a person's spirit surviving after death) — reinforcing two overlapping “spirit” characters into one word is the same doubling strategy behind common words like 喜欢 (“to like”) and 应该 (“should”).

components.note: 石 (rock/stone) — 破 relates to breaking, as a rock can be broken
皮 (pí) gives a loose sound connection to 破's reading pò
土 (earth) — 坏 relates to something crumbling or deteriorating, like broken soil.
不 (bù) reflects an old phonetic link that has largely faded in the modern pronunciation huài.

example.hanzi: 大雨破坏了我们的旅行计划。
example.pinyin: Dàyǔ pòhuài le wǒmen de lǚxíng jìhuà.
example.english: The heavy rain ruined our travel plans.
example.fact: 破坏 extends easily from physical destruction (破坏建筑, “destroy a building”) to abstract damage (破坏关系, “damage a relationship”; 破坏计划, “ruin a plan”) — a metaphorical extension from physical breaking to abstract harm that mirrors how English “wreck” or “ruin” work.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the source of speech.
八 here suggests something small or simple leaving the mouth, giving 只 its meaning 'only, merely.'
The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.hanzi: 他只不过是个孩子,别太严格。
example.pinyin: Tā zhǐbuguò shì ge háizi, bié tài yángé.
example.english: He's just a child, don't be too strict.
example.fact: 只不过 stacks three separate limiting pieces — 只 (“only”), 不 (“not”), 过 (“exceed”) — into one phrase that reads almost like “only not exceeding,” reinforcing a single idea of “merely, no more than” through triple repetition rather than any one character doing the job alone.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — pleasure and delight are feelings of the heart.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match for 愉.
忄 (heart/mind) — the state of mind being described.
夬 (a decisive, resolute action) — a resolute state of mind, giving 快 its meaning 'fast, quick.'

example.hanzi: 祝你旅途愉快!
example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ lǚtú yúkuài!
example.english: Wishing you a pleasant journey!
example.fact: 愉快 is the go-to word for polite, formal well-wishing (祝你...愉快, as in 生日愉快 “happy birthday” or 新年愉快 “happy new year”) — for describing one's own everyday mood in casual speech, 高兴 or 开心 is far more common.

components.note: 火 (fire) — flame at the heart of the picture.
暴 (violent, sudden) — a burst of intense fire, together giving 爆 its meaning 'to explode, burst.'
火 (fire) — 炸 relates to a sudden burst of fire, an explosion.
乍 depicts something happening abruptly — combined with fire, giving 炸 its meaning 'to explode, to deep-fry.'

example.hanzi: 工厂里发生了一次严重的爆炸。
example.pinyin: Gōngchǎng lǐ fāshēng le yí cì yánzhòng de bàozhà.
example.english: A serious explosion occurred at the factory.
example.fact: 爆 and 炸 are near-synonymous “explode” verbs reinforced together in 爆炸, but each also branches off on its own into an everyday food word — 爆 shows up in 爆米花 (“popcorn,” literally “exploded rice flower”) while 炸 shows up in 炸鸡 (“fried chicken”), since deep-frying and exploding share the same sudden burst of heat.

components.note: 辶 (walk/movement) — 迟 describes moving too slowly, arriving 'late.'
尺 (chǐ) gives a sound very close to chí, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 今天早上我又迟到了。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān zǎoshang wǒ yòu chídào le.
example.english: I was late again this morning.
example.fact: 迟到 is a resultative compound — 迟 (“late, slow”) describing the manner, 到 (“to arrive”) naming the result — fusing manner and outcome into one word, the same pattern behind 听到 (“to hear,” literally “listen and succeed”) and 看到 (“to see”).

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — the bottom half of a belt, hanging straight down.
Above the cloth, the strokes crease as if folded at the waist — depicting a belt or sash, the source of 带's meaning 'belt, band,' later 'to bring, carry along.'
土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.

example.hanzi: 请把垃圾带走。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ lājī dàizǒu.
example.english: Please take the trash away.
example.fact: 带走 pairs 带 (“to bring along”) with the directional complement 走 (“to leave, go away”) to mark an item as carried off and away from here, contrasting with 带来 (“to bring here,” 来 = “to come”) — one of many verb pairs built on the same 来/走 “toward/away” opposition.

components.note: 日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'
食 (food) — 餐 relates directly to eating and meals.

example.hanzi: 我们今晚在餐厅吃晚餐。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen jīnwǎn zài cāntīng chī wǎncān.
example.english: We're having dinner at a restaurant tonight.
example.fact: 晚餐 is the more formal, written counterpart to the everyday spoken word 晚饭 (wǎnfàn) for “dinner” — both use 晚 (“evening”) but swap in the more literary 餐 (as in 餐厅 “restaurant”) for the everyday 饭 (“cooked rice, meal”), a register split that recurs across 早餐/早饭 and 午餐/午饭 too.

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
王 (jade, written without its dot) — 玩 originally meant to handle and admire a piece of jade, extending to 'to play, to have fun.'
元 (yuán) gives a sound distantly related to wán, having drifted apart over time.
夭 (a person leaning back) — the pose of someone laughing.
⺮ (bamboo-like strokes) — suggesting a wide grin, giving 笑 its meaning 'to laugh, smile.'

example.hanzi: 别开玩笑了,我是认真的。
example.pinyin: Bié kāi wánxiào le, wǒ shì rènzhēn de.
example.english: Stop joking, I'm serious.
example.fact: 开玩笑 literally means “to open a joke” (开 “to open, start” + 玩笑 “joke, jest”) — treating a joke as something you “open” up, the same verb 开 used for starting a meeting (开会) or turning on a device (开灯), rather than a verb resembling English “to tell” a joke.

meanings: part (in a play or movie etc)

components.note: A drawing of a ridged, pointed animal horn.
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.hanzi: 她在这部电影里演一个重要的角色。
example.pinyin: Tā zài zhè bù diànyǐng lǐ yǎn yí gè zhòngyào de juésè.
example.english: She plays an important role in this movie.
example.fact: 角 is polyphonic: it's read jiǎo for a physical horn, corner, or angle (角度, jiǎodù, “angle”), but jué for a dramatic or social role, as in 角色 — a pronunciation split that tracks the character's two different meanings, though dictionaries also record some speakers reading 角色 as jiǎosè, especially in traditional opera.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 脑 refers to the brain, a part of the body
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 你脑子里在想什么?
example.pinyin: Nǐ nǎozi lǐ zài xiǎng shénme?
example.english: What are you thinking about?
example.fact: 脑子 covers both the literal organ and a metaphorical “mind, wits” (脑子好, “sharp-minded”; 没脑子, “brainless, thoughtless”) — for the strictly anatomical or medical sense, 大脑 (“cerebrum, brain”) is the more precise, formal term.

components.note: 足 (foot) — relates to 路's meaning 'road, path,' something walked on with feet.
各 (gè) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lù.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 我们在路上聊了很多。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài lùshang liáo le hěn duō.
example.english: We talked a lot on the way.
example.fact: 路上 pairs 路 (“road, path”) with the light suffix 上 (“on, upon”) to mean not just physically “on a road” but generally “en route, during the journey” (路上小心, “be careful on your way”) — the same 上-suffix pattern that turns 车 (“car”) into 车上 (“in the car”) or 网 (“net”) into 网上 (“online”).

components.note: 冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'
The 田-shaped top pictures a large, strange head.
儿-shaped legs below trace a crouching, spindly body, together giving 鬼 the shape of a ghostly figure.

example.hanzi: 见鬼,我把钥匙忘在家里了!
example.pinyin: Jiànguǐ, wǒ bǎ yàoshi wàng zài jiā lǐ le!
example.english: Damn it, I forgot my keys at home!
example.fact: 见鬼 literally means “to see a ghost” (见 “to see” + 鬼 “ghost”) — much like English “what the hell” or “damn it” invoke something cursed or otherworldly to voice frustration, Chinese reaches for the same supernatural image via a ghost sighting.

components.note: 士 (a scholar/gentleman) — represents a person of learning and ambition.
心 (heart/mind) — the mind and aspirations of a scholar gave 志 its meaning 'purpose, will, ambition.'

example.hanzi: 她喜欢在等车的时候看杂志。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zài děng chē de shíhou kàn zázhì.
example.english: She likes reading magazines while waiting for the bus.
example.fact: 杂志 combines 杂 (“miscellaneous, mixed”) with 志 (“record, chronicle”) — literally “a mixed record,” describing a periodical that bundles varied articles and topics under one cover, unlike a single-subject book.

components.note: 卩 (a person) — the one being dressed.
月 (a garment shape) — a hand 又 placing a coat on the person, giving 服 its meaning 'clothes; to obey, submit.'

example.hanzi: 这家酒店的服务很周到。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā jiǔdiàn de fúwù hěn zhōudào.
example.english: This hotel's service is very thoughtful.
example.fact: 服务 functions as both a verb and a noun with no change in form (服务顾客, “to serve customers” vs. 好的服务, “good service”) — the same free noun/verb flexibility found in the common word 工作 (“to work” / “a job”); many two-character verbs in Mandarin cross between verb and noun this way, where English often needs a different word for each role.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — 适 relates to fitting well as one moves along, i.e. being suitable
舌 (shé) gives a sound distantly related to 适's reading shì, having drifted apart over a long time

example.hanzi: 这件衣服的大小很合适。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu de dàxiǎo hěn héshì.
example.english: This piece of clothing fits well in size.
example.fact: 合适 (a stative adjective, “X is suitable/fitting”) is easily confused with the similar-sounding verb 适合 (shìhé, “to suit, to be suitable for Y”) — the two share the same two characters in reversed order and overlapping meaning, but 合适 is typically used predicatively while 适合 takes a direct object.

components.note: 冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 我每天都学习两个小时汉语。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān dōu xuéxí liǎng gè xiǎoshí Hànyǔ.
example.english: I study Chinese for two hours every day.
example.fact: 学习 covers both classroom study and broader self-improvement (向他学习, “to learn from him, to follow his example”) — a breadth of use wider than English “to study,” which normally implies formal academic work rather than learning an attitude or skill from someone else.

components.note: 勹 (an enclosing shape) — wrapping around.
巳 (a baby) — swaddled inside, the image of wrapping something up giving 包 its meaning 'to wrap; bag, package.'
扌 (hand) — 括 describes gathering or bundling things together by hand.
舌 (shé) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern pronunciation kuò has diverged considerably.

example.hanzi: 这个价格包括早餐。
example.pinyin: Zhège jiàgé bāokuò zǎocān.
example.english: This price includes breakfast.
example.fact: 包 alone already means “to wrap, to contain” and 括 alone means “to bundle, gather together” — 包括 reinforces two near-synonymous “encompassing” verbs into one word, the same word-building strategy behind common words like 喜欢 (“to like”) and 应该 (“should”).

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汽 relates to water in its vapor form, steam.
气 (rising wisps) — depicts vapor drifting upward, together giving 汽 its meaning 'steam, gas.'
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 他买了一辆新汽车。
example.pinyin: Tā mǎi le yí liàng xīn qìchē.
example.english: He bought a new car.
example.fact: 汽车 literally means “steam vehicle” (汽 “steam, vapor” + 车 “vehicle”) — a name coined in the era of steam-powered engines that stuck even after cars switched to internal combustion, much like English “car” itself outlived its horse-drawn “carriage” origins.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
刂 (a knife) — 刻 relates to carving with a blade
亥 (hài) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches 刻's modern reading kè

example.hanzi: 这是历史上最重要的时刻之一。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì lìshǐ shàng zuì zhòngyào de shíkè zhī yī.
example.english: This is one of the most important moments in history.
example.fact: 时刻 names one precise, often significant point in time (关键时刻, “critical moment”) — a sharper, more formal sense than the everyday, duration-focused 时间 (“time, duration”). As a standalone adverb, 时刻 can also mean “constantly, at every moment” (时刻准备着, “always ready”).

components.note: 广 depicts a lean-to shelter built against a wall or cliff, open on one side — the image behind its meaning 'wide, spacious' and its use as the 'building' radical.
口 (mouth) — the act of speaking.
牛 (ox) — traditionally read as speaking with the forceful weight of an ox, giving 告 its meaning 'to tell, announce, inform.'

example.hanzi: 电视上有很多广告。
example.pinyin: Diànshì shàng yǒu hěn duō guǎnggào.
example.english: There are a lot of commercials on TV.
example.fact: 广告 literally means “to broadly proclaim” (广 “wide, broad” + 告 “to announce, tell” — the same 告 found in 告诉, “to tell”) — a transparent compositional image of spreading a message far and wide that lines up neatly with the word's modern advertising sense.

components.note: 哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.hanzi: 哥们,好久不见!
example.pinyin: Gēmen, hǎojiǔ bú jiàn!
example.english: Bro, long time no see!
example.fact: 哥们 reuses the plural suffix 们 (also seen in 我们, 你们, 他们) on the singular noun 哥 (“older brother”) to address one close male friend, not literally “brothers” as a group — in fast casual speech it's often further softened with a retroflex 儿 as 哥们儿 (gēmenr), especially in Beijing-area Mandarin.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 英 originally meant 'flower, blossom,' later borrowed for 'outstanding, hero' and to write 'England, English.'
央 (yāng) gives a sound hint — 英 is pronounced yīng, sharing the initial consonant and a nasal final, though the vowel has shifted.
囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.

example.hanzi: 他去年去了英国留学。
example.pinyin: Tā qùnián qù le Yīngguó liúxué.
example.english: He went to the UK to study abroad last year.
example.fact: 英 in 英国 is a phonetic borrowing chosen for its sound (approximating “Eng-” in “England”), not for its literal meaning “outstanding, flower” — the same phonetic strategy used to name most foreign countries in Chinese.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笨 originally related to the plain, unworked core of bamboo, later extending to mean dull or clumsy.
本 (běn) gives a sound close to bèn, sharing the same rhyme with a shifted tone.
虫 (a small creature) — 蛋 names an egg, historically grouped together with small creatures like insects and reptiles.
延 (yán) is only distantly related in sound to dàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.hanzi: 别叫我笨蛋,我只是不知道答案。
example.pinyin: Bié jiào wǒ bèndàn, wǒ zhǐshì bù zhīdào dá'àn.
example.english: Don't call me an idiot, I just don't know the answer.
example.fact: 笨蛋 combines “clumsy, dull” (笨) with “egg” (蛋) — 蛋 shows up as a mildly derogatory suffix in several insults (坏蛋 “bad egg, scoundrel”; 混蛋 “jerk”), a productive pattern where calling someone a kind of “egg” in Chinese carries a similar dismissive punch to English “you idiot.”

components.note: 木 (tree) — 相 pictures looking closely at a tree.
目 (eye) — staring closely at a tree to examine it gave 相 the meaning 'to observe' or, later, 'each other, mutual.'

example.hanzi: 这次考试相当难。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì kǎoshì xiāngdāng nán.
example.english: This exam was quite difficult.
example.fact: 相当 does double duty as a comparison verb (“to be equivalent to,” 他的水平相当于大学生, “his level is equivalent to a college student's”) and, more commonly in daily speech, as a degree adverb before an adjective (“quite, fairly,” 相当难) — a split between a literal “matching” sense and a bleached-out intensifier sense.

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
平 depicts a balance scale drawn level and symmetrical — a simple picture of flatness and equality.

example.hanzi: 这个决定对大家都很公平。
example.pinyin: Zhège juédìng duì dàjiā dōu hěn gōngpíng.
example.english: This decision is fair to everyone.
example.fact: 公 contributes its core sense of “public, shared, impartial” — the opposite of 私 (“private, selfish”) — which combines with 平 (“level, even”) to build the compositional image behind 公平: everyone treated on the same, evenly balanced footing.

meanings: trick (in a performance, stage show, acrobatics etc)

components.note: 王 (jade, written without its dot) — 玩 originally meant to handle and admire a piece of jade, extending to 'to play, to have fun.'
元 (yuán) gives a sound distantly related to wán, having drifted apart over time.
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.hanzi: 我不知道这个玩意是干什么用的。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bù zhīdào zhège wányì shì gàn shénme yòng de.
example.english: I don't know what this thing is used for.
example.fact: 玩意 — especially common with the Beijing-flavored retroflex suffix as 玩意儿 (wányìr) — is a mildly dismissive, colloquial way to call an unspecified object “thing, whatsit,” and can extend beyond physical objects to name a performer's “trick or stunt” in a show.

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 保护自然环境是每个人的责任。
example.pinyin: Bǎohù zìrán huánjìng shì měi gè rén de zérèn.
example.english: Protecting the natural environment is everyone's responsibility.
example.fact: 自然 literally reads as “self so” or “of itself, so” (自 “self” + 然 “thus, so”). The compound has roots in Daoist philosophy, where it named “the way things are of themselves, without artificial interference” (as in the phrase 道法自然) — a sense that later broadened into today's everyday word for “nature.”

components.note: 厤 (relating to the sequence of time) — 历 relates to history and the calendar
力 (lì) gives the sound — 历 is pronounced lì, an exact match
乂 (a hand holding a writing tool) — the act of recording events, giving 史 its meaning 'history, chronicle.'

example.hanzi: 中国有着悠久的历史。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó yǒuzhe yōujiǔ de lìshǐ.
example.english: China has a long history.
example.fact: 史 alone already means “history, chronicle” — traditionally analyzed as a hand holding a writing tool, the official scribe who recorded events — and 历史 reinforces that meaning with 历 (“to pass through, experience”), so the compound literally frames history as “what has been experienced and recorded.”

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'
广 depicts a roofed building or shelter.
廷 depicts an open court or hall — together with the shelter above, giving 庭 its meaning 'courtyard, hall.'

example.hanzi: 这个案子下周将在法庭审理。
example.pinyin: Zhège ànzi xiàzhōu jiāng zài fǎtíng shěnlǐ.
example.english: This case will be tried in court next week.
example.fact: 法庭 typically names the tribunal or courtroom where a case is actually heard (上法庭, “to go to court, to appear in court”), while the related 法院 names the broader judicial institution or courthouse — a distinction roughly similar to English “courtroom” vs. “courthouse.”

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俱 describes people being 'all together.'
具 (jù) gives the sound — an exact match for 俱.
乐 is the simplified form of 樂, which depicted a wooden 木 instrument strung with strings 幺, played with a pick 白 — music came to represent joy, giving 乐 its meaning 'happy, music.'
阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).

example.hanzi: 他每周都去健身俱乐部锻炼。
example.pinyin: Tā měi zhōu dōu qù jiànshēn jùlèbù duànliàn.
example.english: He goes to the gym club to exercise every week.
example.fact: 俱乐部 is a phonetic transliteration of English “club” (the syllables jù-lè-bù approximate the sound) — the characters happen to also form a loosely plausible meaning, roughly “all-happy department,” a fortunate bonus rather than the main reason they were picked, as is typical when Chinese absorbs a foreign loanword by sound first.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, movement) — 通 relates to passing through or getting somewhere.
甬 (yǒng) gives a hint of the sound — 通 is pronounced tōng, a connection that has shifted over time.
巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 我通常六点起床。
example.pinyin: Wǒ tōngcháng liù diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: I usually get up at six.
example.fact: 通常 is a fairly neutral, slightly formal way to say “usually” — in casual speech 一般 often does the same job — and 通常 more often opens a sentence as a set-up before describing an exception to it.

components.note: 扌 depicts a hand.
丞 depicts two hands lifting someone out of a pit — paired with another hand, the image is of rescuing someone, giving 拯 its meaning 'to rescue, to save.'
攵 (a hand taking action) — 救 describes the act of rescuing someone.
求 (qiú) gives a sound close to jiù, sharing a similar rhyme.

example.hanzi: 医生成功地拯救了他的生命。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng chénggōng de zhěngjiù le tā de shēngmìng.
example.english: The doctor successfully saved his life.
example.fact: 拯救 is a formal, often dramatic word for rescue (拯救世界, “to save the world”; 拯救生命, “to save a life”) reserved for high-stakes or literary contexts — for an everyday, physical rescue like pulling someone out of the water, plain 救 or 救人 is the far more common choice.

components.note: 羊 (sheep) — work involving livestock, done imperfectly
工 (work) — the labor itself, linked to the idea of falling short
灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.

example.hanzi: 我差点忘了带钱包。
example.pinyin: Wǒ chàdiǎn wàng le dài qiánbāo.
example.english: I almost forgot to bring my wallet.
example.fact: 差点 + verb usually implies a narrowly avoided outcome when the event is undesirable (差点摔倒, “almost fell”) but a narrowly missed one when the event is desirable (差点赢了, “almost won”) — the same phrase covers both a lucky near-miss and an unlucky near-miss, with only context telling the two apart.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 啤 relates to a drink.
卑 (bēi) gives a sound related to 啤's reading pí, though the consonant and vowel have both shifted somewhat.
酉 (a wine jar) — the vessel holding the drink
氵 (liquid) — the wine itself inside the jar

example.hanzi: 这个夏天我们喝了很多啤酒。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiàtiān wǒmen hē le hěn duō píjiǔ.
example.english: We drank a lot of beer this summer.
example.fact: 啤酒 splices sound and meaning: 啤 was coined purely to approximate the sound of a foreign word like “beer/bier,” while 酒 supplies the actual meaning, “alcoholic drink” — a hybrid pattern different from the pure-sound transliteration seen in 俱乐部 (also in this batch, rank 740).

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — 球 originally referred to a round piece of jade, extended to mean 'ball, sphere'
求 (qiú) gives the sound — 球 is also pronounced qiú, an exact match

example.hanzi: 地球是我们唯一的家。
example.pinyin: Dìqiú shì wǒmen wéiyī de jiā.
example.english: Earth is our only home.
example.fact: 球 traces back to a root meaning “a round piece of jade,” later extended to any sphere or ball — so 地球 literally reads as “earth-sphere,” the same 球 that names 篮球 (“basketball”) and 足球 (“soccer”), all riding on its core “round object” sense.

components.note: 爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'

example.hanzi: 警方正在调查这起事故的受害者。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ shìgù de shòuhàizhě.
example.english: Police are investigating the victims of this accident.
example.fact: 受害者 is built from three transparent pieces — 受 (“to receive, suffer”), 害 (“harm”), 者 (“one who...,” a common agent-noun suffix) — literally “one who suffers harm”; that same 者 suffix builds a whole family of role-nouns like 记者 (“journalist,” one who records) and 读者 (“reader,” one who reads).

components.note: Heart/mind — foolishness is related to one's mind.
Gives the sound yú, matching the character's reading.
虫 (worm, insect) — 蠢 originally described the wriggling movement of insects.
春 (chūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 蠢, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 那是一个非常愚蠢的决定。
example.pinyin: Nà shì yí gè fēicháng yúchǔn de juédìng.
example.english: That was a very stupid decision.
example.fact: 愚 and 蠢 are both independently “foolish, dull” and get reinforced together in 愚蠢, but 蠢's own etymology — built on 虫 (“insect”), evoking the wriggling, aimless movement of bugs — supplies a vivid, almost literal image behind calling a decision or person “stupid.”

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炸 relates to a sudden burst of fire, an explosion.
乍 depicts something happening abruptly — combined with fire, giving 炸 its meaning 'to explode, to deep-fry.'
弓 (bow) — 弹 relates to a projectile shot from a bow, like a pellet
单 (dān) gives a loose sound connection to 弹's reading dàn

example.hanzi: 士兵们在路边发现了一个炸弹。
example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen zài lùbiān fāxiàn le yí gè zhàdàn.
example.english: The soldiers found a bomb by the roadside.
example.fact: 弹 (dàn) alone names any small, self-contained projectile — from 子弹 (“bullet”) to 导弹 (“guided missile”) to 炸弹 here — while 炸 (also seen in 爆炸, also in this batch, rank 714) supplies the “explosive” half, so 炸弹 literally reads as “exploding projectile.”

components.note: 耳 (ear) — 联 originally meant 'connected, linked,' perhaps through the image of joined loops.
关 (guān) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lián.
丰 depicts a plant heavy with grain, a picture of abundance and plenty.
阝 (a settlement or region) — together with 丰, the image of an abundant place gave 邦 its meaning 'nation, state.'

example.hanzi: 美国是一个联邦制国家。
example.pinyin: Měiguó shì yí gè liánbāngzhì guójiā.
example.english: The United States is a federal country.
example.fact: 邦 is an older, literary word for “state, nation” on its own that survives today mainly inside compounds like 联邦 (“federation,” literally “linked/joined states”) and 邦交 (“diplomatic relations between states”), rather than as an everyday standalone word.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 评 relates to speaking judgments or opinions about something
平 (píng) gives the sound — an exact match with 评's reading píng

example.hanzi: 三位评委都给了她很高的分数。
example.pinyin: Sān wèi píngwěi dōu gěi le tā hěn gāo de fēnshù.
example.english: All three judges gave her a very high score.
example.fact: 评委 fuses 评 (“to judge, evaluate,” as in 评论 “commentary”) with 委, short for 委员 (“committee member”) — and despite naming a role tied to a group, 评委 in everyday speech is used just as often for one individual panel judge (一位评委, “one judge”) as for the panel collectively.
